title: The Breath You Keep: A Simple Cue for the Hard Part of a Lift
subtitle: When a repetition gets difficult, breathing can become an afterthought. A flexible cue—keep air moving—offers a useful alternative to rigid rules about exactly when to inhale or exhale.
imageAlt: Two friends of different ages lifting dumbbells side by side in a bright gym, each focused on their own movement and breathing.
imageConcept: A candid, close-but-unposed view of two friends at adjacent dumbbell benches: one in mid-repetition, the other beginning a set, both breathing naturally and concentrating on their own lifts. Show different ages without implying one person is coaching the other.
body:
A set can feel straightforward until the last few repetitions. Then shoulders tighten, the face strains, and a breath that was happening without thought may suddenly stop. That pause can feel like concentration: brace, push, finish. But breathing is part of the effort, not a detail to remember only after the weight is back on the rack.

A practical cue is simple: keep breathing through the repetition. It does not require a universal rule that says inhale on the way down and exhale on the way up. People differ in exercise, load, experience and comfort. The aim is to notice an unintended breath-hold and avoid turning it into the default response to difficulty.
A lift is not a resting blood-pressure reading

Blood pressure is not fixed from one moment to the next. During a demanding muscular effort, the cardiovascular system responds to the work being done; a reading taken at rest does not describe every second of a challenging set. A review of resistance exercise research describes substantial arterial-pressure changes during some lifting efforts, with effort and breathing among the factors that can contribute [1].

That context matters in both directions. A temporary response during a lift is not the same thing as a diagnosis of high blood pressure. And evidence that regular exercise can support cardiovascular health does not mean a particular breathing cue treats hypertension. The useful takeaway is narrower: breathe regularly, manage effort, and keep exercise habits distinct from medical care.
What the breathing study actually found

A small 1992 experiment examined 20 novice male weightlifters performing arm curls and knee extensions. Breath-holding produced the highest blood-pressure responses. When the participants inhaled rather than exhaled during the lifting phase, however, the measured elevations were similar [2].

That result supports caution about holding the breath, not a one-size-fits-all breathing choreography. The study was limited in size, participants and exercises; it cannot establish what will happen for every person or every lift. It also did not show that a particular breathing pattern prevents a dangerous response. Its practical contribution is modest and helpful: if a rigid inhale-exhale formula makes a lift feel awkward, regular breathing is a more defensible starting point than forcing that formula.
Try a cue, not a script

Before a set, take a moment to settle your stance and notice whether your breathing feels easy. As you move, let the breath continue rather than clamping down automatically when the repetition becomes hard. Some lifters will naturally exhale during the effort and inhale as they return; others may find a different rhythm more comfortable. Neither needs to become a test of doing the movement correctly.

If you catch yourself holding your breath, do not panic or rush to compensate mid-repetition. Finish or stop the movement in a controlled way, reset, and try again with a lighter load or an easier variation if needed. You can also rest longer between sets. The goal is a repeatable effort in which you can stay attentive—not to push through a weight that makes controlled movement or breathing difficult.

A useful self-check is to ask after a set: Did I keep breathing, or did I brace and forget? That observation can guide the next set without turning every repetition into a performance review.

Start with a familiar exercise and a load you can move with control. Before the first repetition, decide on one reminder—“keep breathing” or simply “don’t hold”—rather than trying to monitor several technical instructions at once. Perform the movement at a steady pace that feels manageable. If you notice breath-holding as the effort rises, end the set at a controlled point, rest, and adjust the weight or number of repetitions.

For a new exercise, practice the movement with no weight or a lighter load before making it challenging. That gives you room to coordinate breathing and movement without also wrestling with a demanding effort. If training with a partner, agree on a simple signal to pause or stop; the partner’s role is not to police someone’s breath but to help keep the set safe and communicative.

The American Heart Association advises breathing regularly during warm-up, exercise and cool-down, noting that breath-holding can raise blood pressure and cause cramping [3]. If you repeatedly find yourself straining or unable to breathe comfortably during a set, treat that as useful feedback to reduce the challenge, not as a cue to force more effort.
Strength training belongs in the bigger picture

The long-term question is different from what happens during one hard repetition. 

Strength work can still be a meaningful part of an active life. A sustainable plan can begin with manageable movements and progress as ability and circumstances allow.

Breathing well does not mean every set will feel effortless, and a breath-hold is not a reason to diagnose yourself. It is a signal to pay attention to how the load, pace and movement are fitting together. Choose a version of the exercise that lets you stay controlled, and build from there.

People with cardiovascular disease or another pre-existing condition should check with a healthcare professional before beginning or changing activity, as the American Heart Association advises [3]. If you have questions about blood pressure, medication or whether a training plan is appropriate, bring them to a qualified clinician rather than trying to answer them through a breathing technique. The cue is useful precisely because it stays modest: keep breathing, adjust the effort when needed, and let strength training be one part of broader care.
